parts.title: Passage 1 · How New York Became America's Largest City
parts.instructions: Follow the original instructions and word limits shown on the book pages. Choose the requested letters or write your answers.

questions.explanation: Routes are the paths or areas travelled along between places.
questions.evidence: trade routes from the ports to the central regions

questions.explanation: Freight means goods transported from one place to another.
questions.evidence: moving heavy freight very far

questions.explanation: A strip is a long, narrow piece of something.
questions.evidence: a long strip of low land

questions.explanation: Regions are areas of a country.
questions.evidence: the central regions of the country

questions.explanation: 'Consequently' introduces a result, so it means 'as a result'.
questions.evidence: Exports from New York were greater than imports. Consequently ...

questions.explanation: Section 1 introduces geography, history and economics as the three factors explaining the city's growth.
questions.evidence: geography, history, and economics

questions.explanation: Section 2 describes seaports as places where goods enter and leave the country.
questions.evidence: around seaports

questions.explanation: Section 3 says a favourable location alone does not explain the growth of a great industrial city.
questions.evidence: needed more than their geographical location

questions.explanation: Section 5 follows the canal's completion with the extension of the inland water transport network.
questions.evidence: a great inland shipping system

questions.explanation: Section 6 deals with the arrival of the railroads and their effect on transport.
questions.evidence: The coming of the railroads

questions.explanation: Section 7 explains why shipping companies could offer cheap passenger journeys from Europe.
questions.evidence: Passengers could come from Europe very cheaply

questions.explanation: Section 8 focuses on New York as the major arrival port for people from Europe.
questions.evidence: the greatest port for receiving people from European countries

questions.explanation: Section 3 explicitly rejects the idea that geographical location by itself made cities such as New York great industrial centres.
questions.evidence: needed more than their geographical location

questions.explanation: The passage says people had already moved west by about 1815, then describes wagons used to carry freight. It does not specify how those people travelled.
questions.evidence: many Americans ... had already moved toward the west ... moving heavy freight

questions.explanation: A canal seemed the best solution in New York State, but the text does not report agreement by every American.
questions.evidence: In New York State, a canal seemed the best solution

questions.explanation: The canal followed the low land from the eastern end of Lake Erie to the Hudson River.
questions.evidence: From the eastern end of Lake Erie ... to the Hudson River ... Here the Erie Canal was constructed.

questions.explanation: Freight costs fell immediately to about one tenth of their former level.
questions.evidence: The canal produced an immediate effect. Freight costs were cut to about one tenth

questions.explanation: The arrival of railroads made canal shipping less important.
questions.evidence: The coming of the railroads made canal shipping less important

questions.explanation: The final section directly credits the newcomers' labour with helping the city become great.
questions.evidence: Their labour helped the city become great.

parts.title: Passage 2 · Public Libraries
parts.instructions: Follow the original instructions and word limits shown on the book pages. Choose the requested letters or write your answers.

questions.explanation: To charge a fee is to ask for it as payment.
questions.evidence: It charges no fee for its services.

questions.explanation: To loan a book is to lend it, rather than borrow or sell it.
questions.evidence: The library loans its materials.

questions.explanation: Donated money is given freely, without repayment being required.
questions.evidence: money that has been donated

questions.explanation: Here 'indicated' means pointed out or made known.
questions.evidence: people in that city had indicated they found useful

questions.explanation: Paragraph A introduces the library as a free service for everyone in the community.
questions.evidence: for all the people in a community ... charges no fee

questions.explanation: Paragraph B describes the money supporting libraries: taxes, donations and gifts.
questions.evidence: tax-supported ... money that has been donated

questions.explanation: Paragraph C compares libraries of different shapes, sizes and collection sizes.
questions.evidence: Few public libraries are exactly alike.

questions.explanation: Paragraph D explains the similar ways libraries divide and arrange books, including age groups and fiction versus nonfiction.
questions.evidence: arrange their books and other materials in similar ways

questions.explanation: Paragraph E explains that reference books remain inside the library.
questions.evidence: Reference books are never to be taken out

questions.explanation: Paragraph F says each library decides how to organise special collections according to local needs.
questions.evidence: Each library decides for itself

questions.explanation: Paragraph G explains how the community's interests shape the library's holdings. Morgan horses are an example, not the whole topic.
questions.evidence: reflect the community's special interests

questions.explanation: The sentence in paragraph A says the service is for everyone in a community.
questions.evidence: for all the people in a community to use

questions.explanation: Materials can be borrowed for a particular, limited period.
questions.evidence: taken out for a specific time

questions.explanation: Paragraph B lists taxes alongside donated money and gifts as sources of financial support.
questions.evidence: part of their money from taxes and part from gifts

questions.explanation: These are the two age-group labels used in paragraph D. The answer follows the wording of the passage.
questions.evidence: two basic age groups, children and adult

questions.explanation: Reference books must remain in the library building.
questions.evidence: Reference books are never to be taken out of the library building.

questions.explanation: Paragraph F says some nonfiction materials may be placed in a special area or a separate room. Either phrase fits the word limit.
questions.evidence: a special area or separate room

questions.explanation: The holdings reflect the subjects the local community is especially interested in.
questions.evidence: reflect the community's special interests
